such eomplaint unltil the hon. 'member mentioned it to me this evening, but, since that organization was formed, when I received a complaint of any kind I immediately communicated it to Mr. W. M. Neal, secretary of the organization, and it did not matter whether that complaint was in regard to shortage of cars or trouble at any point, I .always received an immediate reply and assistance was at once forthcoming, or the matter in regard to which the complaint was made was taken up by the association and promptly dealt with.

As I have said, the heads of that organization are the presidents of the railways. Some of the men on the subcommittee are: Sir George Bury_ representing the Canadian Pacific; Mr. Gillen, representing the Grand Trunk; Mr. Hanna, representing the Canadian Northern; Mr. A. E. Warren, representing the minister here at Ottawa; and Mr. Hayes, representing the Government railways. I think Sir George Bury, Mr. Hanna, Mr. Gillen, and the rest of those gentlemen will ibear me out when I say that they have done everything possible to operate the railways during the past winter practically as one system, and to give the very best service and assistance in their power as operators, and as the railways themselves could Tender. I wish at this point to give those men all the credit that is due to them. At the present time they are carrying on that organization and doing everything they possibly can. I should not like the impression to go out that the railways had notj during the past year, been operated to their fullest capacity. I should like it to be known that in my opinion those men, from the president down to the humblest man on the railways, have, during last year, worked harder and had better co-operation than at any previous time in the history of the railways of Canada. I believe they all realized that, on account of this war, it was their duty, as men, to do all they could. I believe they did their work sincerely and honestly; they are continuing to do so now, and they will continue to do so as long as this war is going on.	.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I did not wish to attack the association, and I do not wish to oppose the purchasing by the Government of the equipment necessary for our railways. I do not object to that at all. I think, however, it is a matter of amazement for the public to see the Government of this country giving the railways financial assistance to purchase engines, while at junction points everybody is at liberty to see many engines lying idle, and when you ask why all those engines are lying idle there, thus diminishing the hauling power of our railways, you are told the reason is that the railways of this country are unable to secure the skilled labour necessary to overhaul those engines. If that is the reason why you often see trains with two engines when one should be able to do the work, my opinion is that instead of purchasing new engines, it would be better for the Government to supply skilled labourers to overhaul those engines in order that the
greatest tonnage might be hauled. That is the point I am endeavouring to make.
Mr. J. D. REID; Might I ask the hon. member at what point he saw so many engines lying idle? The reason I ask is this: Complaints of that kind should be brought to the attention of the organization. If the hon. member will tell me on what road and at what points those engines are lying idle, I shall be able to explain the matter when my estimates come up in a few days from now.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
When the minister brings down his estimates, I shall be able to give him all the information. It is a matter of public notoriety, even in our province, that at all junction points you see those engines lying idle. When you travel, you will come across two engines hauling a train when one engine is generally able to do the work.
Mr. A. K, MACLEAN: That is because the engines are not sufficiently strong in motive power. The railways have not been able to purchase engines of sufficient stiengtfh to operate their trains. During the last year or two they have not been purchasing a sufficient number of locomotives. Therefore the condition the hon. gentleman describes might very well happen. Railway companies in 'Canada during the last year have had to operate trains with engines which in ordinary times they would use in their yards, or which would be engaged in light and unimportant work.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: The explanation of my hon. friend may he all right; but when your curiosity is excited by seeing two engines hauling a train and you inquire into the hauling capacity of each engine, and you make the addition of the tonnage, land when you are told the reason why there are two engines on the train is because the engines are not properly overhauled, t'he explanation of the minister does not fill the bill.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I should like again to ask the hon. member to tell me at what point on any railway he has seen a number of engines lying idle since October last, and I shall tell him the reason why. Time and again during the last month or ,so I have had up in my office the head officials of the Grand Trunk railway company. I have had Mr. Robb, who is the general master mechanic of the Grand Trunk railway company, and Mr. Robb assured me that every engine of the Grand Trunk rail-



way was in operation and that there was no trouble to keep them in repair. Therefore, from the statements made to me by the Grand Trunk officials, I do not believe that it is on that railway that engines have been lying idle since October last. As to the Canadian Northern, Mr. Hanna tells me that all their engines have been in operation and they have had no trouble making repairs when necessary. So far as the Government railways are concerned, the officials tell me they can keep their engines in repair, and they have sufficient men tx>
do so. I cannot for one moment believe that the Canadian Government railways have any engines lying idle at any point on the system. Therefore, from the information before me, and not having heard from the Canadian Pacific, I conclude that if engines have been lying idle since October last it must have been on the Canadian Pacific. In discussing matters with the Secretary of the Canadian Railway Association for National Defence, I was informed that the railways had used all their equipment. The question came up whether the Canadian Pacific could loan four engines to the Algona Central railway, and Jhey would only consent to loan them on condition that we gave them four of the new engines in their place; that is the way I understand it. It was the greatest surprise to me this evening to be told that on any of the railway systems of Canada there have been a lot of engines lying idle since last October. It is such an important matter that I think the hon. member should give me the names iof the different railways, so that tl can take the matter up with the Canadian Railway Association for Naional Defence and ascertain why engines were allowed to remain on the railways unrepaired. .

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: I will supply that information at the proper time.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman should let me have it now, so that I can give him a reply when my estimates are up.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
Before six o'clock I
urged the Minister of Railways to fix a limit to the amount required for the equipment of these railways', and I am glad that this evening the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K. IMaclean) promised the committee that when the Bill founded upon this resolution is introduced my suggestion will be considered; I am quite satisfied with that. In view of that_ I think the minister should amend his resolution because, as it stands, it is still a very large order. It reads:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that during the present war and for one year thereafter,-
I think everybody will agree that during the course of this war we shall have to come to the aid of all the railway companies of Canada with the possible exception of the Canadian Pacific. I quite admit that this equipment will be more urgently required during the winter months on account of the heavy traffic. But I do think the minister should amend his resolution to read as follows:	.
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that during the next fiscal year,-
And so on. The minister knows that every railway company prepares an annual budget, just as the Government does, and estimates its requirements for the coming fiscal year, and it would be quite easy for my hon. friend to thus estimate his requirements of rolling stock.
In fact, if you read the annual report of any railway company, you get the data about the requirements of that company. I repeat, this is a very large order. Nobody
35i
objects to helping the railways during the present emergency; on the contrary, the people are quite ready to commit their Government to the aid required by the railway companies in order to facilitate the transportation system. But this is, after all, a money Bill. Whether the Finance Minister is called upon to give cash, 'or to issue treasury bills, or to endorse notes, or to sign bonds, or to sign equipment bonds, the-credit of the country is none the less engaged. Being a money Bill, we cannot amend it by decreasing it, because we do not know the amount which will be required by my hon. friend under this resolution. We could, however, decrease the amount if we knew it. At all events, my hon. friend can easily find out from the companies wt"*t help they require from the Government in the matter of equipment for the next current year, and with that information at hand he can say about what amount wall be involved during that period. Otherwise my honourable friend is not amenable to Parliament; he puts himself above His Majesty the King. His Majesty the King, requiring supplies from Parliament, states the amount in the estimates, and each item is checked and debated. But, my hon. friend is above the King. He comes and asks, not for a limited sum, but for any amount during the present war and for one year thereafter. If my hon. friend will amend his resolution and provide that there will be a stated annual amount based on the estimates which he will receive from the railway companies, he will meet no opposition in the House, because everybody is anxious to help the transportation system.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance explained that if the resolution is allowed to go through he will introduce the Bill, and when we get into committee we can amend it there.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Amend it in what respect?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: We can then consider amending it in so far as limiting the amount is concerned.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I was glad to hear the hon. Acting Minister of Finance say, in answer to my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding), that he proposes to limit the appropriation. But I would call the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that he must do it on .the

resolution, because he cannot do it afterward.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Because the Bill is founded on the resolution and you must limit the amount that you are asking Parliament to vote by your resolution.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: The Bill must not authorize a greater amount than was authorized by the resolution. There being no amount stated in the resolution, it would seem to 'be perfectly proper for the Bill to put a limitation to the amount. Therefore, I do not think there will be any violation of the rule.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: There would certainly ibe a violation of the rule. The rule is that no blank cheque can be given to the Government. They must state what they ask of the people to spend, and if they ask for a limited appropriation, a fixed amount, that certainly must be put in the resolution. The point is worth considering.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: I have not examined the point particularly, but I would think that if a resolution, upon which a Bill is to be founded, authorized an expenditure of $100,000,000, the amount could be reduced in the Bill to $50,000,000.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Exactly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: That is the absolute point which the Acting Minister of Finance has made.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: He says that inasmuch as there is no limit in the resolution you may nevertheless properly put a limit in the Bill, and that is what he proposes to do.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: If you have a money Bill it must be founded on a resolution to limit the amount that may be expended. You may decrease it, but you cannot increase it.	.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: I suppose, in discussing this railway question, the Prince Edward Island railway is 'considered as part of the Intercolonial railway?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: It is part of the Canadian Government railway system.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
It appears to me that this resolution calls for the expenditure of the whole of the consolidated fund of Canada that is not appropriated. My hon. friend has pointed out a great many diffi-
['Sir Wilfrid iLaurier.]
culties that have been encountered in connection with the transportation question of Canada during the past year. I mentioned on a previous occasion that this transportation question is one of the most important which comes before the Parliament of Canada to-day. It is all very fine for people to talk about increasing production on the farms, but it is of no use to increase production on the farms if you cannot move the product. In my province the whole railway system is in the cellar and has been for the last four years. The fact is demonstrated by the acts of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. J. D. Reid) in providing four new narrow gauge locomotives for a railway which in the natural course of events will cease to toe a narrow-gauge railway in the very near future. I am not blaming the Government for that.
I want to say a word about Mr. Hayes, the General Manager of the Canadian Government Railway System. I know him very well and I have had a great deal of 'business with him. He is the most capable gentleman that ever at any time handled the Canadian Government Railways. When Mr. Hayes told me he was going to order these four locomotives, he igaid, "I suppose you will object to them?" I replied, "Not by any means; it is the best thing you can do to tide over a situation which at present is unbearable."
But, Sir, there is a better way of obviating the difficulties on the Prince Edward Island 'railroad, and I want to draw the attention of the Minister of Railways to what I am going to say in this regard. Notwithstanding that I am not an expert-like my hon. friend across the House who has been riding on the railroads for a long time-I know what I am talking about because I am an old transportation man. I want to tell the minister that the best way to obviate the difficulties on the Prince Edward Island railway with reference to rolling -stock and engines is to widen the gauge of that railway, or supply a third rail between Port Borden and Summerside and Port Borden and Charlottetown. That will accomplish results very much better than by buying a lot of narrow gauge cars and narrow gauge engines that we would have to re-sell within the next two or three years.
While I am on this subject I would like to ask the minister whether the Reid-New-foundland railway system has prerempted, or done anything towards purchasing, the narrow gauge rolling stock and locomotives on our system, when we dispose of it.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I have not heard of
the Reid-Newfoundland railway making any proposition with respect to the purchase of any narrow gauge equipment on our railways, because we would not consider it for one moment until the existing gauge has been widened. I can say to the hon. gentleman there has been no proposition whatever of the nature to which he alludes.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: The minister knows as well as I do that the Reid-Newfoundland system is narrow gauge like the Prince Edward Island railway. He knows further that a promise has been made to us, which the right hon. leader of the Government is going to implement as soon as he can, to widen or standardize the gauge of the Prince Edward Island railway. Otherwise he will lose the credit which 'he is getting to-day for having provided the Prince Edward Island car ferry system. Our narrow gauge system in Prince Edward Island is owned by the Dominion Government, hut it was paid for by the people of that province, a fact which some members of this House ought to know when the affairs of Prince Edward Island are being discussed, and allusion is made to the railway deficits, and all that sort of thing. We paid for the Prince Edward Island railway ourselves and presented the Dominion Government with it. The Government may say, "All right, take it hack," hut that is not the question. We will take the railway back if the Government will give us the money that is due to us, for you must remember that when we went into Confederation the Dominion owed us five or six million dollars, and that was the money with which the railroad was built.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
If this were not somewhat of a war measure I certainly would put myself upon record against the resolution, because it really places too much power in the bands of a minister. However, if it is to he considered in any way as a war measure I want to give my ready assent to it. Before doing so I call the attention of the Minister of Railways to the fact that under the Appropriation Act of 1916 we have already paid the Canadian Northern $15,000,000. The minister , informs us that so far by way of equipment we have given over to the Canadian Northern some $22,500,000.
I would like to know from him whether anything else has been given to that company, by way of equipment, material, or rolling stock?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
That is all that has been given to the Canadian Northern. We are purchasing some rails and that company
will get some of those as well as the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific systems.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: That is apart altogether from the $22,500,000 which the Canadian Northern have already received during the current year?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: The $22,500,000 of equipment will 'be paid during the present fiscal year. We have not yet bought any equipment of any kind.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: But contracts have been placed?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Not for the Canadian Northern, except as regards the contracts I read a few moments ago.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: What about the message cabled over by the Government directly to the boys in .the trenches about the Order " totalling $22,500,000, and' the bulk of it being made up of cars for the Canadian Northern railway?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: That is all included in the figures to which I have referred.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Has the minister in contemplation the purchasing of further roiling stock for the Canadian Northern for the coming year?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
Outside of what I read to-night, the only equipment that I contemplate purchasing is as follows: A requisition has been made on me to purchase ten or fifteen snow ploughs, which might probably cost another $100,000. Then I have been urged by the National Railway Defence Association, the organization representing all of the railways in Canada, to purchase one hundred tourist cars. At the present time, speaking from memory, there are probably six or seven hundred cars owned by all the railways in Canada that are available for the transport of troops to and from the .seaboard, and I have been discussing the proposed purchase of one hundred additional cars with Sir George Bury, the head of the Canadian Pacific railway, with a view to ascertaining if we cannot get along without any more equipment of the kind. We have also been asked to purchase nineteen baggage cars to be used in connection with the movement of troop trains to and fro, and it may be requisite to acquire a few more-things of that kind.
As to the suggestion of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) (that I limit the scope of this motion, I would move * that the resolution, be amended by adding the following words:

Provided, however, that the expenditure in any one fiscal year under this resolution shall not exceed the sum of fifty million dollars.
I mention that amount for the reason that we have 100,000 tons of rails ordered.
I may have to purchase some more equipment such as I mentioned a little while ago. That is not a very large amount over what we have really contracted for, and if the hon. member will accept this amende ment I would like the resolution to be moved.
Mr. LEM1IEUX: Certainly, I accept the amendment for myself. But I hope that when the Bill to be founded on this resolution comes before the House, my hon. friend will be able to give an approximate estimate of what is to he expended during the present fiscal year.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Of course, I will be glad to do that. I shall give the hon. member all the information I can.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: While the hon. minister is on this question, will' he kindly let us know how many of the 25,000 cars which were in the United States a few weeks ago are still there? According to a statement of the hon. Minister of Public Works, in a speech he made in New York or Boston, they had 25,000 of our cars down there. Have we got them back yet?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: There has been an excess of Canadian cars in the United States over and above the number of American cars in Canada. The highest number at any one time was, about twenty-three or twenty-four thousand. I have been pressing, and the Canadian railways have been doing everything they could to get the cars back, but the car shortage in the United States has been ao great that any cars sent over there we could not. get back, and the number increased until it reached twenty-five thousand, and the shippers in Canada were suffering because we could not get our cars back. We had to refuse to allow Canadian cars to go over to the United States until we got the number over there reduced. Ffiom time to time the number was reduced, and if my memory serves me right in the last report I had, a week or so ago, the number was down to about eleven thousand. If we had those cars in Canada we would not have any shortage of cars to supply the public.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
Before this resolution goes thro-ugh, I would like to point out that the hon. minister's amendment furuier strengthens my opposition to the measure. It is further evidence to me that the Minister
[Mr. J. I). Reid.I
of Railways- and Canals should not undertake the management o-f this great railway system of Canada. He is able here, in five minutes, to make his estimates for an indefinite period, from now until the war is over, and for a year after that. How does he know that he will not require $51,000,000 next year, or $25,000,000, or any other sum ? It is altogether too large an order, stepping out here with a fifty-million-dollar-a-year resolution. I think that the Government should take the matter under consideration and come to some determination as to what they intend to do with the railway situation in this country, before we go on spending these millions toy the fifties ot hundreds.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
If I may be permitted, and
if I may make bold to do so, I would like to offer a word of advice to the Minister of Railways. I have had some experience as a .railway man, not as my bon. friend from East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) on the engines of a railway, but as- a maintenance of way main on the roadbed of the Canadian Pacific. I would like to point out to the minister what, in my opinion, seems to be the necessity for the vast expenditure on equipment of the railways at the present time. The whole trouble, lies- in. the fact that the TO-adbed of these different railways is in poor condition, and has been so for a -great number of years. I think it would be well, if it -c-omes under the- jurisdiction of the Minister of Railways, to see that these roadbeds are put into proper shape, and I know that if that is done not nearly the amount of money which is- being asked for will (be required in the -future to kee-p the rolling stock in condition. I know conditions in the West, because I have travelled over the- Canadian Northern to some extent, and I know that, the roadbed is in poor shape; in fact, I happened to be in a wreck on one of the 'branch lines of the Canadian Northern near Winnipeg; and in that wreck some seven or eight freight cars were derailed, and- they were simply lifted aside with a lifting machine and burned on the ground. Now, that is occurring all. over Canada at the present time on the .Canadian Northern system, and, I believe, on the other Government systems in, the Dominion. If the roadbeds were put into proper shape the engines at present used on these different roads would be able to pull double the number of ears they are pulling -at the present time. I understand that in the West, on some sections of the Canadian Northern system, the engines are pulling something like twenty or twenty-five cars, and that is the

utmost they can pull. An engine, if it is any good at all, on a good roadbed, on the prairie sections of the road in Manitoba and the West, should pull at least fifty to sixty cars loaded to capacity. 1 say that it the roadbeds are put into proper shape it [DOT]will be. of great assistance to the Government in financing and in providing for the rolling stock of these different railroads. The whole trouble lies in the fact that the roadbeds are not kept in proper shape. I suppose, if 'I began to discuss the labour question, and what the Government intends to do in regard to it, I would be driving away from the question, so I shall not take up that phase of the matter at this time, but on another occasion >1 may have something to say on this point.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: I do not think it is fair that the hon. minister should ask us to give the Government a blank cheque of fifty million dollars. We are sent here by our constituents to vote what definite amounts should be spent this year and next year and each year. The Government might just as well ask us once for all to vote them as much money as they want, iand let us go back home. The Government should respect the people, and inform their representatives what they intend to spend, and how they intend to spend it, giving details. The Government comes to the House with an estimate of $250,000,000, with another estimate of $500,000,000, and now we are asked for $50,000,000 more. They are spending money as if it were peanuts. I am opposed to this method of doing business. No company would do business on such a basis. Before we go further with this resolution, Mr. Chairman, I submit that for the benefit of members of the committee and the people of the country we should have more detailed information on the subject.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
This resolution will authorize the Minister of Railways to buy a good deal of equipment; in fact, orders have already been placed for such equipment. The National Railway Defence Association appears to be taking good care of the engines, but I do not know that they have taken as good care of the freight cars. On the way from Montreal a month ago any one could see in the yards many freight cars, empty, some with missing doors, some with parts of the roofs off- cars which could have been repaired very easily and put back in the service to help relieve the shortage of equipment. Many of these cars now lying idle could easily
be repaired at Moncton. The Canadian Government railways own and operate big shops, some of which are not used at all, or practically not used. Take, for instance, the Canadian Government shops at Riviere du Loup. These shops, which were built at great expense, are now lying idle; why are they not used for the repairing of freight cars in order to relieve the situation? I understand also that many of our freight cars are used in various parts of the country for storing freight. For very little money sheds could be erected and these cars could be unloaded and put back into service. Last winter, the member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Gauthier) told the House some engines had been left idle and that a great many cars had been left loaded in the big yards because of the lack of water facilities. Take, for instance, in Mont-magny, where there are a few miles of track and siding, and where I have seen five or six freight trains at a time delayed on account of lack of water facilities. Often the engineers have to run their engines from Montmagny up the hill to St. Pierre to get water; then they cut the train in two, leave part at Montmagny, and do not come back to Montmagny to get the other part of the train. This difficulty exists on account of water facilities not being placed at Montmagny, and consequently much traffic is not properly taken care of. The minister says that $50,000,000 or thereabouts will be sufficient to help relieve the situation during the next fiscal year. That is quite a sum. He has already ordered $35,000,000 worth of equipment; to this he adds $15,-000,000-what for? We do not know. He wants the committee to adopt a provision under which $50,000,000 may be appropriated each year during the war, and one year thereafter. Surely it is in order to provide a sufficient amount for the next fiscal year, and if when Parliament meets, nine or ten months hence, more money is required, then we will grant, perhaps, another $50,000,000. That is a safe procedure; it is better than providing for the expenditure of $50,000,000 a year for an indefinite number of years. When will the war end? Will it be considered as ended when the men cease fighting at the front, or when the treaty of peace is signed? Or will it ha ended by Order in Council passed by this Government under the War Measures Act? So far as I can see, anything at all can be done under that Act. I do- not think it would be safe for this committee to vote so many millions under the plan suggested. I think

the position taken by the member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) is very wise, and that many members of the House will support it.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: The minister told us tonight before six o'clock that he had placed an order for 60,000 cars and 150 engines. According to the resolution, a considerable number of cars will be added to the stock already purchased. Has an estimate been made of the number of cars that will be required, and has any inquiry been made as to the possibility of building the cars, the number of shops now working, and the number of cars which can be turned out each year? I put this question to the minister because I have sent him a letter written to me by a gentleman from Three Rivers who has had considerable experience in car building and who is ready and willing if the order is placed with him, to deliver ten freight cars a day five months from this date, provided the order justifies the manufacture. Surely this amount is not asked haphazard; some estimate must have been taken of future requirements of the railways which desire to procure equipment from the Government. Has any estimate been given to the Minister of Railways as to the number of cars that the railway companies are short or the number of cars that may be required for transportation during this year? If so, are the cars so required to be ordered through the Minister of Railways, and has he any idea what apportionment is to be made to the di^erent companies of the various kinds of cars-flat cars, coal cars, tank cars, and so on mentioned in the statement the minister read to the House this afternoon?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
Before ordering any equipment at all, I got together in my office the heads of the Canadian Northern railway, the Grand Trunk railway and the Canadian Government railway system, and we had a discussion as to the quantity of equipment that would be required during the present fiscal year, so that the railways could haul next season's crop and also he in a position to be operated to their full capacity during the coming winter. After going over the matter with those gentlemen, we gave an order for the equipment, a list of which I have given to the House. Each railway, of course, stated what it would require, and I have given that statement. In Canada, there are companies that manufacture cars that have a capacity very much larger than necessary to fill our orders. I see by the press, and, in fact, I know,

that the Canada Car and Foundry Company have received a very large order from the United States Government, because the United States Government are giving veTy large orders for cars for the railways of that country. The United States Government are doing practically the same as we are doing in this regard. In this time of war, it is not in the interest of the country that railway companies should go on to the market with their bonds. I shall be very glad to give the hon. member further detailed information if necessary, but I think the information I have given covers all the questions he has asked. This equipment will be distributed amongst our own Canadian railways.
.Mr. BUREAU: The Grand Trunk is the only one that is not under Government control.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: The Canadian Northern, while it is owned by the Government, is being operated as a private corporation. There is the Grand Trunk railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific railway.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: That is under Government control.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Not yet.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
Partly.
* Mr. J. D. REID: The Quebec Southern, which I think is owned by the Delaware and Hudson, requires a few rails. The Canadian Pacific, under this legislation, will get 300 miles of rails, two or three million dollars' worth of the purchases we propose making. They will, of course, pay cash for what they receive; at least we expect they will. It will be seen, therefore, that we are purchasing equipment that will be used by the several railways.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Do the Grand Trunk, the Delaware and Hudson and the Canadian Pacific prefer to have the 'Government buy their equipment for them? Are they not capable of purchasing their own equipment?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I mentioned the Canadian Pacific for this reason. The Canadian Pacific have been trying to purchase rails. There are only two companies in Canada that make rails, and the Canadian Pacific could not purchase rails from those companies because they were manufacturing munitions. The Government arranged with the Dominion Iron and Steel Company to change their plant from what they were manufacturing and to supply 100,000 tons of rails. We purchased that ourselves, and we intend to distribute it amongst the several railways.

Mr. MeCREA:	Do the several railways
prefer to have it done in that way?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
Yes. they asked that
it. be done in that way.
Mr. MeCREA: The minister told ns that early this season 20,000 Canadian cars were in the States, .and that the latest report he had was that that number had been reduced to about 11,000. Can the minister give any information as to horw many foreign cars are in Canada?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
There are, in the
United States, 25,000 Canadian cars in excess of foreign cars in Canada.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
At the present time the
country is suffering from the lack of care and also from a lack of passenger accommodation. That portion of the country which I represent and a part of the country represented by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro). containing a population of approximately 150,000 people, is back to the old days again of construction; they get one train in the morning and one train at night.
Mr. MeCREA: The hon. member should be glad to have that.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I want to know from the minister if there is .any possibility of this war board giving any better passenger accommodation than has been given, or if it is going to be.like a new "cop" on the corner, stopping all the traffic.
With reference to freight cars, I know that so far as shipping during last winter, is concerned, the shortage of cars' occasioned a loss to shippers in Ontario of thousands of dollars daily. A concern in which I am interested had no less than 27 carloads of steel tied up between Buffalo and Col-lingwood, the amount involved being close on a quarter of a million dollars, and that shipment was tied up for weeks and weeks. Something must be wrong. We know, of course, that the snow was pretty bad, but I 'was held up on a passenger train, travelling thirty miles in two days, and in that thirty miles there was not a snow drift that stopped the train for three minutes. There were four snow-ploughs ahead of us. What was wrong? The crews? When the Bill comes before the House, the labour question will have to be discussed, because we all know that the men have been giving service to the railroads for a great deal lees money than is paid to men in any other department of business in the country.
In regard to this resolution, I am pleased that the minister has limited the amount,
because I think it is asking Parliament to go a very long way to give any minister of the Crown in such a democratic country as this a blank cheque on the treasury. That has never been done in the history of British parliamentary institutions, and I do not think we should establish a precedent. Further than that, I do not think it is a good precedent to establish an annual vote for years ahead. Are we going to give up all our parliamentary functions? Is Parliament going to cease to exist? Is Parliament going to go out of business altogether and give a blank cheque to each of the ministers of the Crown to carry on business- until a year after the war? I say with all seriousness, that this war may continue for four or five years. If one reads the papers this evening, the conclusion of the war looks as far off as it did two years ago. For that reason, I think the minister should hesitate. This Parliament has never refused a Minister of Railways or any other minister any reasonable request for funds that has ever been placed before it. There is no reason why we should give up all our functions to a star chamber and allow any department of Government to have a blank cheque up to fifty million dollars a year from now on to the end of the war I believe in- British institutions. I believe in maintaining the constitution of this country, and to do that I think we should carry on in war time the same as at any other time. There are too many people going around the country wanting this fad and that fad on account of the war, and men are wanting to sell corn cures and this, that and the other thing to help win the war. This Parliament is asked to vote $50,000,000 until the conclusion of the war for no other reason than that it is in connection with the railways on account of the war. I think the minister will be well advised when bringing down the Bill to limit the time to the fiscal year. I think there will be a few of us, <at all events, left for next session; we do not expect the Germans to come and take possession Of the country before then, and as we shall have another session of Parliament, the minister could bring down another vote next year. I am not opposing this vote, but I am opposing the unconstitutional features of it. The first thing .about the resolution that struck me, and which I could hardly swallow, was that it was giving the minister a blank cheque. The second feature to which I objected was that it was good during the war and for one year thereafter. Something might be said in its favour if this were for a foreign

(expenditure during a war period, but Parliament is quite able to cope with domestic expenditures of this kind by voting an *amount annually.
Mr. MgGRiBA: Unquestionably there has *been a great shortage of both power and oars. The hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) has complained about the passenger service. No doubt it is not what we should like to have, but I have never heard of a man having to wait for a week for a *passenger train, as has frequently happened in the case of freight shipments. *The passenger service has been curtailed, *but on the whole I think the needs of the *people are well taken care of. We are certainly nlot so badly off in that matter as we are in respect to freight. There is a great quantity of freight to be moved, and there is evidently a severe shortage of cars. *One gentleman has said this evening that the sidings are filled with empty cars out of commission, but I think you will find that these cars are of an old type and of light capacity, and therefore not safe for heavy traffic.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: The hon. member is a very large shipper. Has he been able to get all the empty cars he wants in which to ship his freight, or is he a month behind with his orders?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: I certainly agree that there is a shortage. That is the point I was trying to make.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Everybody says the same.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I think the minister was justified in bringing down this measure in order to supply the needs of'this country. What I was not clear about was whether the Canadian Pacific, the Delaware and Hudson, and the other roads who are able to take care of themselves were satisfied with this arrangement, but the minister assures me that they are, so that is all right.
What the shippers want is
10 p.m. means of transporting their goods, and I think'the minister will be well advised to proceed as quickly as possible to provide the required equipment and rolling stock to carry on the business of the country. I must say, however,, that it is not wise to give carte blanche even to the Minister of Railways. The minister might amend his resolution limiting the period to one year, and then he could ask for another vote next session, and it would he quite in order for the House to give it. But I do not think he should ask to be given carte blanche for an unlimited period, and without any restrictions on the expenditure.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Replying to my hon, friend from North Simcoe, the passenger service has undoubtedly been curtailed during the past year.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Is it going to be increased this summer?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
The hon. member wishes us to increase the passenger service in Canada. Let me tell him why the passenger service was curtailed, and no one knows it better than my hon. friend. We have a lot of troops to transport to the seaboard, and a lot of men to bring back, and it was necessary for the railroads to cut down their .passenger traffic in order to provide the necessary cars and engines for this purpose. The position of the board of railway commissioners, of which J approve, was that we should take all the passenger cars we could possibly get and use them for war purposes during the war. We cannot build ears in a day; it takes time. . All the roads have had instructions to decrease the passenger traffic as much as possible in order to .provide cars for the purposes I have mentioned. That has been the policy, and so long as this traffic continues, we must have the cars. Let me give one instance where extra passenger cars have been, required. A very large number of cars

perhaps I should not mention just how many-have been required to bring a great many thousands of Chinese from the Pacific to the Atlantic coast on their way *overseas. We had to take ears from some ' of our systems for this service, and the passenger traffic was decreased on certain roads. The hon. member for North Simcoe asks whether he will get a better service during the coming year. I say to him that when the traffic of which I have spoken ceases I am willing to urge the railway commission to give him a better service on his road, but if it is necessary to- transport troops from the Pacific to the Atlantic in order to help the (boys at the front, then my hon. friend's passenger service will be decreased, if necessary, in order that we may get the ears. The coal situation also accounts for a further decrease in the number of cars. The railways, were taxed to their utmost in order to get fuel to the different parts of Ontario, and, in fact, throughout the whole Dominion. I can say, having gone into this matter, and being in touch from day to day with the organization in Montreal, that I believe the heads of the different railways have done everything possible to give the best service they could to all parts of the Domin-

ion. during the last year and they will continue to do so during the present year if they can possibly spare the cars. But war needs must foe supplied first. I have been dodnig my best, and the railways .have been doing their best, to get cars built during the past year, and the companies I have mentioned have promised to let us have these cars in time for the rush in the fall. The criticism that this resolution is practically giving the Government a blank cheque for a certain length of time, is met,
I think, toy the fact that the amount is lim

ited to $50,000,000, and the period is limited to the duration of the war and. one year thereafter. We all hope the war may end this year, but it may go on for another year. That is a matter that I would like the committee to allow me to consider when we get the Bill in the committee. At all events, it limits the amount to $50,000,000. It is for the war and one year after, but it may possibly be for one, two or three years. It is not for an unlimited time; it is limited by the clause "for the war and one year thereafter." We all hope it will not be for more than one year.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Is it not a fact that in the year 1916 there was double the number of troops moved in this country, and is it not also true, as everybody knows, that there was no slackening in the passenger traffic?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: No, that statement is absolutely incorrect.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
It is correct and everybody knows it.
M. J. D. REID: I say to the hon. member it is not correct.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I want to ask the minister if, when he was making his estimate, he allowed for the extra revenue the railways are going to get by reason of the increase of fifteen per cent in freight rates. I understand the railway commission has permitted the railways to increase their freight rates by fifteen per cent. I had a letter from a western man complaining of the good western Unionists and saying it was going to take at least $20,000,000 out of tne western farmers, and that it served them right. Well, that is all -right. When you were estimating it at $50,000,000, did you allow for the $20,000,000 that you are going to take out of the western grain growers by this increase of fifteen per cent? That only applies to the grain crop. There are the other freights all over Canada and I should think that the fifteen per cent
added to the freight rates is going to give the railways an immense sum. I see the Government penalize the Canadian Pacific to the extent of fifteen per cent showing that they can make both ends meet, like the dog when he was catching the flea. I understand that the Grand Trunk railway last year paid up all their liabilities and that they have been able to expend $26,000,000 in speculation in the last two or three years. These railways are doing all the work they can, and if you are raising tne rates by fifteen per cent they must be getting a big rake-off. I want to know if the minister allowed for this increased revenue that is going to accrue to the railways by reason of the advance in freight rates?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I do not want to be put on record as being opposed to the country getting more rolling stock; quite the reverse. I am only objecting to the system that has allowed the country to be two or three years behind in getting rolling stock. As the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Hay) has pointed out, the roadbed is in bad shape. That will come in for consideration,
I presume, at a later date. But that is another question that is being left a little late. My position is, not that this country does not need rolling stock or repairs to the right of way, or that the maintenance of way should not receive attention, but my complaint is of the system that allows the railways to get into this position before conditions are taken care of. I maintain that under the present system of management we will not have efficiency. I do not find fault with increasing the rolling stock. I know we are short.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: I only heard the minister make a few remarks in reference to the status of the railways. I gathered from him that the Canadian Northern belongs to the Government, but that it is operated by .the Canadian Northern corporation. Is that correct?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: It is.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: It is now the property of the Government?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: We own the stock, but the road is being operated by the Canadian Northern directors.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: There is an arbitration in regard to the majority portion of the stock, is there not?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
The Government have taken over the stock, and therefore own the Canadian Northern isystem. A portion of

the equity is subject to arbitration, and the board of directors are operating the system.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: What is the status of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: The Transcontinental railway between Winnipeg and Moncton is being operated by the Government. It is part of the Canadian Government railway system. The Grand Trunk Pacific is being operated by the board of directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company, a separate corporation controlled by the Grand Trunk Railway company. The Grand Trunk Pacific practically belongs to the Grand Trunk Railway company.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
They are in an entirely different position from the Canadian Northern and the Transcontinental railway which belong to the Government?
M. J. D. REID: Yes,

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: 1 understand the minister to say that this amount that we are asked to authorize, and the expenditure to he made for rolling stock will 'be distributed among the various companies. He also stated that the Government would give to the Canadian Pacific a portion of the rolling stock and that the Government expected the Canadian Pacific to pay them back.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: I said the Canadian Pacific would get a portion of the rails that we had ordered. There are a hundred thousand tons of rails. That is only a portion of the equipment to be purchased under this Bill. Three or four hundred miles of those new rails out of the hundred thousand tons will go to the Canadian Pacific.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: The minister said that it was the expectation of the Government that the Canadian Pacific would pay for those rails,

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: They will pay for them.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I think the House is entitled to a clear and positive declaration, not that that is the expectation, but that the money will be demanded from the Canadian Pacific. That company has a surplus of tens of millions of dollars, in addition to which this Government has granted an increase in rates of fifteen per cent, which will enable the company to increase its earnings by from $20,000,000 to $25,000,000 or $30,000,000. Of course, it is understood that they are to be taxed. As far as my judgment goes, that is somewhat indefinite.
I had hoped that before this stage of the
,
session was reached we would have had a field day on the railway question. The granting of an increase of fifteen per cent to the railways all round will mean an additional direct burden on the people of this country who use transportation, of not less than $30,000,000, and it will mean, in my judgment, an indirect burden upon the people of probably $100,000,000. The moment this increase in rates was announced the price of sugar advanced ten cents a hundred in Winnipeg, and an intimation was given that the price of all commodities would be increased. Merchants will seize this as an opportunity for increasing the price of foodstuffs and staples. That is the tragedy of this increase. Perhaps this is not the time to discuss this question. I should like to have a day to myself to discuss it, but at present I only point out that in so far as the Canadian Pacific is concerned, a wealthy corporation with a surplus of tens of millions, it ought to be very clearly understood by this House and the people of this country that the Government does not propose to use its resources in order to feed that company with millions and millions of dollars' worth of rails and equipment. I feel strongly that we should not give a blank cheque to the Government for an indefinite period. The question as to when the war will close is, in my judgment, a very indefinite one-the war may last ten years, it looks to me as if it will certainly last two or three years anyway-and while we want, and must provide, transportation in this country, still I think that Parliament ought to reserve to itself the right to control the expenditures from session to session.
While il am on my feet and discussing the question of rates, I want to say that
J.	think the result of the increase will bear with especial severity upon the people of the Northwest. After all there is only a limited percentage-
The OHAIiRlMAN: Order. I must ask the hon. gentleman to desist from discussing railroad rates, and the circumstances of the people in the Northwest, because that subject is too far from the scope of the present resolution.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I beg pardon of the Committee, and I will not proceed further on that line. Probably when a field day takes place on this subject we will have the opportunity of expressing our views.
Mr. .1. D. REID: I can say to the hon. member that the Canadian Pacific Railway
company will pay for the rails they get.

Mr. (LEMIEUX: The 'Minister of Railways has mentioned only a few of the companies that may benefit from this resolution in the matter of equipment. He has mentioned the Canadian Northern, the Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Grand Trunk system. Might I ask the minister if some of the branch lines on the Intercolonial which have not been .purchased by the Government and other branch systems in .eastern Canada will also ,be heard if they require any equipment?
While opposing the mode adopted by the minister in presenting this resolution, I am not against the spirit of the resolution itself. On the contrary, I believe that we .must help-lour railway systems to get equipment during these years, especially in view of what occurred last winter when traffic was congested during the hardest months of the year. In that connection, however, might I suggest to my hon. friend an increase in the demurrage charges? Last winter-and I know this because I am identified with the pulip business indirectly-some of the firms with which I am connected could hardly secure any cars because the railway companies were suffering from a shortage, their cars were in the United States and were not being returned. Is there not any possible means by wmch the railway commission in Canada, and the inter-state commerce commission in the United States, could reach an agreement whereby an end would be put to that state of things?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
What do you say as to
reciprocal demurrage?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: That is what we have.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
Let me give you an illustration:	You want coal for your factory
and the railway company switches your coal into a siding half way towards your factory, and leaves it there foT a couple of weeks. Why should you not collect demurrage from the railway company? There are two sides to the demurrage question.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: The Minister of Railways says that he is willing to do so.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: If he had admitted that I would not 'be asking the minister to refrain from taking the power to expend $50,000,000 per year during the balance of the war. There's where I differ from him. The war may last several years, or it may only last a few months, and it is not dignified on the part of the Government to secure holus bolus-I shall not say the benefit of the war because it confers no benefits-^ but during the continuance of the war, unknown as its duration may be, a huge sum of money. I appeal again to my hon. friend to consider the matter very seriously, and to amend his resolution so as to declare that the Government will only expend the $50,000,000 in the one year. Next year he can apply to Parliament again, and he will be as liberally and generously treated as he has been this year.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman asked me a question with respect to branch lines in New Brunswick.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I had reference to those that had not been acquired by the Government.
Mr. ,T. D. REID: There are six or seven of them?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: There is one also in Gaspe.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
Yes, there is one in Gaspe, but all of these railway companies stated last fall that they had not sufficient equipment and were in trouble. I issued instructions at that time to General Manager Hayes to give them all the equip, ment and assistance they needed at any

time to keep their lines- in operation, and the railways in question received that assistance during the whole winter. If these railways wanted the use of our cars we would charge them a certain amount for the privilege, if they wanted to purchase any of our equipment we would let them have it; but really the amount they required altogether was very small. We deal with them as we do with the Canadian Government railways, and they are given engines or cars as they may require them, an arrangement which is perfectly satisfactory, I think, so far as they are concerned.
Now with reference to the resolution, two questions have been raised. One was as to the amount. That was answered several minutes ago, when I moved the amendment.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
There is no objection to that.
Mr. J. 0. REID:	The other question
raised is as to the period toeing for an unlimited time. I stated some time ago that it was for the duration of the war and one year after. I said that when we got into committee I would consider the matter at that time. The Bill, of course, could not go further without being again in committee. However, if it be the wish to. insert it in the Bill -before the Ball has been introduced-I have the Bill here printed and ready-I am willing to limit it to the fiscal year. I do not want to do anything other than what I think is fair. Therefore I [DOT]would a6k that the resolution be made to read as follows:
That it is expedient to provide that during the present fiscal year the Minister of Railways and Canals, with the approval of the Governor in Council, may acquire engines, cars, rails and other railway equipment and materials to an amount not exceeding fifty million dollars-
And so on. That would limit the time to the present fiscal year and the amount to fifty million dollars. I beg to move:
That the resolution be amended by striking out the words "present war and for one year thereafter"-and substituting therefore the words "present fiscal year."

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Would the minister allow me to make a suggestion? Occasionally _ Mr. Chairman, it is the custom, in the case of large public buildings, to grant a total sum, and then vote a certain proportion of that per annum. Might we not provide in this resolution a sum not exceeding $200,000,000 during this present war, and that fifty millions would toe voted for the present fiscal year?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: That has -been the custom. For instance, the parliament buildings estimate was fixed at five million dollars^ and half a million appropriated from year to year.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: That is a different question.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
Parliament is not voting
that amount at all, tout it specifies some sum which may possibly be voted. That was what the 'minister felt in the first place, that he could- not put the omnibus amount in. If he wishes to amend it to fifty millions annually as he has done now, I am quite willing to accede to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
It is moved toy the
Minister of Railways and Canals-:
That the resolution -be amended by striking out in the first and second lines thereof the words "war artd for one year thereafter," and substituting therefor the words 'fiscal year," and by adding in the fourth 1-ine of the said resolution, after the word "materials," the words "to an amount not exceeding fifty million dollars."

Amendment agreed to.
Resolution as amended agreed to.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Might I ae-k the hon. minister if it As the intention of the Govern-men to increase the number of cars in the section between Levis and the east, including the -counties of Montmagny, L'Islet and Kamo-uraska? That section is a farming country, and I noticed last year that the farmers and lumbermen could not get the cars they required.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I took up with the
general manager a short time ago the question of providing cars in the very district mentioned, and he promised me that he would do his very best, and stated that he expected to relieve that situation within a very short time.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether the calculation he has made includes the necessary equipment for the completion of the Hudson Bay railway?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: No, that is not in this item.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
Following the example of the hon, member of L'Islet (Mr. Farfardi, I would like to say a few words regarding conditions in the district of Abitibi. Reading La Presse the other day, I came across an article headed " Colonization in the Abitibi," in which it was stated that there is practically a crisis in that region, that colonization and agriculture cannot be carried on for lack of means of transportation.

I know of a lumber company which has a great deal of lumber and pulpwood ready for shipment, thousands of cords of pulp-wood are ready for delivery, which cannot be sent to the United States, or to the wharves and harbours in this country, for the reason that there is no means of transporting it. I would like to ask the minister if it is his intention to remedy that situation.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: I have had that question up with the board of railway commissioners and with the national defence association, and we have been, doing our best to relieve that situation. As I stated a few moments ago, the whole trouble is that if we send our Canadian cars to the United States we do not get them back, so we are then unable to transport the pulp-wood to the mills in Canada.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: Abitibi is in the northern part of the province of Quebec.

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext: I asked a moment ago if the hon. minister could remedy the situation which existed last winter owing to our cars not being returned promptly from the United States. The exporters of Canada were really in a very difficult position on account of the shortage of cars. The United States keep our cars, and I do not know whether it is that the demurrage is not high enough, but they do not seem to care about returning them promptly. Is there not an arrangement between the interstate commerce commission and the railway commission by which such a state of things can be remedied?

subtopic: ACQUIREMENT BY MINISTER OF RAILWAYS FOR CANADA DURING THE PRESENT WAR.
speechtext:
I may say to the hon. member that it is an impossibility to do more than we have been doing, during the last winter. The board of railway commissioners, and the several railway companies have been doing everything possible to remedy the situation. They have had special men in the United States looking up the cars. We have had our representative Mr. Lloyd Harris, doing his utmost with the American Government, I have personally sent message after message to Mr. McAdoo, urging him to assist _us in getting what we claim to be our just rights. So that the influence of this Government, of the railways and of the railway commission, has been exerted to the utmost to remedy the situation. As a result, as I said before, we have lately been able to reduce the number of cars held in the United States from twenty-five thousand to eleven thousand.
Resolution reported, read the first and second time, and concurred in.
Hon. J. D. REID thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 42, to amend the Department of Railways and Canals Act.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the firsttime.	.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Civil Government-Department of Militia and Defence-salaries, $212,500.
Major General MiEWBURN: The amount of these estimates for the Department of Militia and Defence is so insignificant compared with the amount that we have just been discussing-$50,000,000-that it will not require very much explanation. It is my intention when, at -a very early date, the war estimates are brought before the House, to give a detailed statement of the war policy of the Government, including such information regarding our troops in France, England, and Canada as it is advisable to give from a public standpoint. I do not purpose, therefore, to make a full statement to-night in connection with these estimates, but I shall take advantage of the opportunity of doing so when the war estimates are brought down by the Prime Minister.
['I am perfectly willing\nto agree to that proposal.']
Will the minister please fix a date, say next Tuesday, for this debate?
The Prime Minister told me yesterday that he hoped to bring down the war estimates to-morrowr, if that would suit the convenience of the House.
When may we expect the fourth volume of the Auditor General's Report, containing details of the war expenditure?
I thought it had been laid on the Table.

May I suggest to the Minister of Militia, whom I am glad to see in the House this session for the first time, that he follow the practice that has been followed for the last few years of presenting to the House a detailed statement of the expenditure of money voted for war purposes? During two or three previous sessions-in fact, ever since the wyar began -a special publication has been issued and distributed among the members giving in detail the expenditure of the war appropriation. Without that information it is impossible to discuss intelligently either the expenditure that has been made or the appropriation of $500,000,000 that is asked for

this session. I therefore urge upon my hon. friend the necessity of submitting that information to the committee as soon as possible.
Major-General MEWBURN: The report of the Militia Council is in press now, but the purchases of the Militia Department were made through the war purchasing commission, whose xeport is soon to be laid on the Talble. I fancy that is what the hon. gentleman refers to.

No, not altogether. It is necessary to find what expenditure is made under war appropriation, for instance, whether the cost of certain commissions, of certain boards, of certain offices that have been established, relate to the war appropriation. My reason for pressing this request to-night is that upon searching through the Auditor General's report for information regarding this expenditure-information which would ordinarily be found in that report-I discovered that it was not there. It is impossible, therefore, to ascertain the character of the expenditure under this war appropriation unless this information be given. I have not in mind particular contracts or purchases made through the war purchasing commission, but other expenditures, information regarding which apparently is not available in any other quarter to which I and some of my friends on this side of the House have had access.

I would call the minister's attention to the fact that the only details ,we have as to war expenditure are to be found in the public accounts under war accounts. The details of the war expenditure by the Militia Department are given from 1st April, 1916, to 31st March, 1917. Further than that, we have absolutely no details as to the war expenditures and no way of finding them out, so that we are hardly in a position to vote any estimates until we have fuller information.

I think I realise what my hon. friends are asking for. During the last three years there has been issued a memorandum which is supplementary to the report of the Auditor General. That memorandum, as I understand it, has not been issued this year, the reason being that practically everything that heretofore appeared in the memorandum will now appear in the report of the war purchasing commission. The Minister of Militia, therefore, is not able to give that information to-night. I would suggest that perhaps we might confine our discussion tonight to Civil Government, which is the
[iMr. iMurphy._l
item under discussion, and I am sure the minister, when the matter comes up on the next occasion, will be able to give the House all the necessary information.

d agree with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) that to-night the discussion, on which we have not yet entered, should be confined tp the proposed appropriation immediately before the Committee. But might I also point out that a statement of the transactions carried out by the war purchasing commission will not give the House information as to what has been paid for salaries, for instance, for salaries in connection with the board of food control or in connection with the central appeal judge's office and matters of that kind which I understand are taken out en bloc of this war appropriation? It is item's of that kind, in regard to which it has been found difficult to get information.	.

That is quite true, and the House is certainly entitled to all that information. That, of course, would not appear in the report of the war purchasing commission, which would give only the actual purchases. There will however be another way of getting at it.

The Minister of Militia will find no difficulty with his estimates, if, after discussion with his deputy minister, he gets that detailed statement for which, since the beginning of the war, we have been accustomed to ask. The affairs of the Militia Department have increased so much that the estimates which are before the House are not sufficiently explicit for hon. members. I may say to the minister that he will find no difficulty in having his estimates passed, because he has the good will of the House and has always, since the opening of the session, answered very willingly and generously the requests made to him. But to facilitate the work of the Committee, we certainly require this detailed statement, which the minister's predecessor used to distribute each time his estimates came up before the House. I agree that as regards Civil Government, this statement is not so much needed.

I can assure the hon. member that that statement will -be forthcoming. It is probably due to ignorance on my part that it has not been distributed. As to the memorandum published last- year, all purchases of the Militia Department which have been made by the war purchasing commission will be included in its report, which is in process of preparation.
When will it be ready?

We have
every day been asking the war purchasing commission to expedite it. As regards salaries and expenses paid in connection with the tribunals under the Military Service Act, no money had been paid out by the Department of Militia and Defence in connection with the operation of that Act.
